content: 1. A randomized trial was conducted to evaluate the outcomes of individuals who report sexual activity with women. The study was published in the journal Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2011, volume 87, issue 5, pages 399–405. 2. Neumann M, O’Donnell L, Doval A, Schillinger J, Blank S, Ortiz-Rios E, and colleagues investigated the effectiveness of the VOICES/ VOCES intervention for the prevention of sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) when implemented by health department staff. The study assessed its applicability in real-world settings and was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2011, volume 38, issue 2, pages 133–139. 3. Patterson TL, Mausbach B, Lozada R, Staines-Orozco H, Semple SJ, Fraga-Vallejo M, and colleagues evaluated the efficacy of a brief behavioral intervention aimed at promoting condom use among female sex workers in Tijuana and Ciudad Juarez, Mexico. The findings were published in the American Journal of Public Health in 2008, volume 98, issue 11, pages 2051–2057. 4. Thrun M, Cook PF, Bradley-Springer LA, Gardner L, Marks G, Wright J, and colleagues implemented a multisite, clinic-based intervention called Positive STEPs to improve prevention counseling provided by HIV care providers. The results were published in AIDS Education and Prevention in February 2009, volume 21, issue 1, pages 55–66. 5. Warner L, Klausner JD, Rietmeijer CA, Malotte CK, O’Donnell L, Margolis AD, and colleagues examined the impact of a brief video intervention on the incidence of infections among patients attending sexually transmitted disease clinics. The study was published in PLoS Medicine in 2008, volume 5, issue 6, article e135. 6. The guideline development process for the document involved a range of participants, including Igor Toskin from the Department of Reproductive Health and Research at WHO, Geneva, who served as the coordinator. The WHO Steering Group included experts such as Tomas John Allen, Moazzam Ali, Venkatraman Chandra-Mouli, Mary Eluned Gaffield, Claudia García-Moreno, Antonio Carlos Gerbase, Metin Gülmezoglu, Beverly Jane Ferguson, Vladimir Poznyak, and Igor Toskin, all affiliated with WHO in Geneva. 7. The systematic review group included Bergen Hope Cooper (WHO Consultant, USA), Regina Kulier (Fondation PROFA, Switzerland), and Igor Toskin (WHO, Geneva). Regina Kulier also served as the GRADE methodologist. 8. Barbara Klugman, Co-Chair of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and affiliated with the School of Public Health, Faculty of Health Sciences, University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa, contributed as the writer of the guideline document. 9. Members of the Guideline Development Group included Tamara Adrián-Hernandez (Adrian & Adrian Abogados Consultores, Venezuela), Elham Atalla (Sexual Health Services, Ministry of Health, Bahrain), George Ayala (Global Forum on MSM & HIV, USA), John Munroe Douglas (CDC, USA), Emily Maria Godfrey (University of Washington School of Medicine, USA), Sharful Islam Khan (icddr,b, Bangladesh), Barbara Klugman (University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa), Charlotta Löfgren-Mårtenson (Malmö University, Sweden), Geetanjali Misra (CREA, India), Patanjali Dev Nayar (WHO/South-East Asia), Rafael Mazin Reynoso (WHO/Americas), Thierry Troussier (UNESCO Chair, France), Marlene Frieda Wasserman (Sexual Medicine Consultant, South Africa), and Christine Winkelmann (Federal Centre for Health Education, Germany). 10. The PICO framework (Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes) was used to guide the systematic review. Three PICO questions were identified by the Guideline Development Group to structure the evidence review. These questions addressed the effectiveness of interventions in promoting sexual well-being, the impact of sensitization/training programs for primary healthcare providers on knowledge and skills in sexuality counseling, and the use of educational techniques to enhance patient understanding of sexual health issues. 11. The systematic review included studies evaluating various outcomes such as STI/HIV prevention, unintended pregnancies, sexual concerns, self-esteem, efficacy, knowledge, attitudes, and skills. The studies reviewed spanned a range of populations, including adolescents and adults, and assessed the use of materials and educational techniques in clinical and community settings.
